source.title: AdaPPA: Adaptive Position Pre-Fill Jailbreak Attack Approach Targeting LLMs
source.authors: Lijia Lv; Weigang Zhang; Xuehai Tang; Jie Wen; Feng Liu; Ji-Zhong Han; Songlin Hu

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Figure 2 is referenced and captioned, but its plotted values are not available in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures harmful-request attack success under position pre-filling, a different implementation of the opening-prefill bypass mechanism. It does not measure the original study’s per-token KL quantity.
record.gate_note: The paper reports ASR for AdaPPA and for safe-prefill combinations, which bear on V4. Its method aggregates six prompt combinations in Table I. Table II reports separate safe-prefill combinations. Figure 2 is described as comparing fill conditions, but its plotted values are unavailable. Baseline attack results in Table I are not extracted as rows because they are other attack methods, not measurements of the claimed prefill mechanism.
record.test_reason: This is an attack-method paper. It cites shallow alignment (arXiv:2406.05946) as motivation and reports its own method's ASR, mostly against other attacks (Table I). It reports no numeric unfilled or no-prefill baseline, so the readable results cannot show whether prefilling a compliant start defeats refusal beyond baseline. Figure 2 has an Unfilled condition, but its values are not in the text. AdaPPA also mixes in question rewriting and safe-response pivots. For the black-box GPT models, the text does not say whether the 'pre-fill' sits in the assistant turn or inside the user prompt.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that pre-filling the output with adaptive safe-then-harmful content exploits shallow alignment and outperforms TAP, PAP and FuzzLLM on black-box models. They claim a 47% gain on Llama2.
record.recipe_differences: It tests the position-prefill bypass idea using AdaPPA: generated and segmented safe and harmful text, sometimes combined with rewritten questions and transitional phrases. Table I aggregates six prompt combinations; it is not the original per-token KL measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: On ChatGLM3-6B, ASR varies across original versus rewritten questions and across safe/harmful filler combinations (Table II). The authors also state that different pre-fill lengths significantly affect attack vulnerability, but Figure 2's plotted values are unavailable in the supplied text.

fits_no_version.finding: On ChatGLM3-6B, adding a safe response and a transition before the harmful prefill roughly doubles ASR. With the original question it rises from 0.27–0.30 to 0.57–0.65; with the rewritten question from 0.49–0.55 to 0.72–0.74.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A pseudo-termination (a safe answer followed by a pivot) placed before harmful continuation weakens refusal more than a harmful prefill alone.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing
record.problems: No numerical unfilled baseline is reported in the supplied text for Figure 2, and Table II compares prefill combinations rather than prefill against an unfilled condition. Table I aggregates six prompt combinations into one value per model. The paper does not state uncertainty estimates or the number of AdvBench test questions.
record.rows_left_out: Table I comparator attack results for TAP, PAP and FuzzLLM are omitted because they are other methods, not results of the prefill mechanism itself. Table II's X+1/3H, X+2/3H and X+H conditions are omitted because they do not include a safe/compliant prefill. Figure 2 is retained as r17, but its numeric values cannot be extracted from the supplied text.

untested.parts: Prefill against a numeric no-prefill baseline is not reported in text; adversarial suffixes and decoding changes are not tested.

missing.what: Harmful-only prefill ASRs (X+1/3H, X+2/3H, X+H: 0.298/0.292/0.271 for Q; 0.485/0.546/0.508 for R). These are the conditions closest to V4's compliant-start prefill, and the record wrongly omitted them.
missing.versions: V4 (would still need an unfilled baseline)

missing.what: Plotted ASR for Unfilled vs Generic/Adaptive/Safe Termination/Hybrid fill on ChatGLM3-6B; values are needed for any V4 verdict.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests' label rests on own-method ASRs with no unfilled baseline, so I reclassified the study as T4. Table I baselines also differ in iterations (50 vs one round of six combinations). Judging used Llama Guard 2 plus manual review. The AdvBench sample size is not stated. The paper claims ten models but lists eight families.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning of the target safety-trained models on harmful examples is tested.
No fine-tuning of target models on benign instruction data is tested.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL measurement is reported.
The study tests pre-filled prompts, not adversarial suffixes or decoding changes.
No weight or rank localization of safety behavior is tested.
The paper invokes shallow alignment as motivation but does not test whether data or training objectives cause shallowness.
No training intended to deepen safety is tested.
